newsitem.title: UK: Art industry takes to Internet to catch thieves.
newsitem.headline: Art industry takes to Internet to catch thieves.

text.p: The art world is taking to the information superhighway to catch robbers who have turned international art theft into a thriving business.
Art experts say the worldwide trade in looted works of art is worth at least $1 billion a year and is now only exceeded by drug deals and the illicit arms business.
Now police, auctioneers and collectors hope to stem the growing trade by placing advertisements for stolen works on the Internet.
Trace Magazine, a leading tool of the international art community in tracking down stolen paintings and antiques, has gone electronic because thieves are moving swiftly from country to country.
"It is one of the fastest growing crimes in the world and has become so international. Things move out of the country so quickly," said Colin Norvell-Read of Trace Magazine.
"So many of the pieces move out and turn up in Germany, France or the United States," he told Reuters on Wednesday.
Eastern Europe has become a particularly fast growing market since the fall of communism and the rise in organised crime.
The global trade from art robberies is now huge and diamonds and jewellery, which are hard to trace, have become illegal currency for terrorists and drug barons, art experts say.
So Trace is hoping to keep one step ahead electronically.
"All our advertisements are now going on the Internet. It was a logical extension of the hard copy from the magazine," Norvell-Read said.

As a member of the Thesaurus Information group, Trace is also being linked to what Norvell-Read called "the world's largest database site for art and antiques, which is regularly used by some 2,000 people daily".
The database gives details of all auctions being held around the world.

"Using the Internet will be invaluable as dealers can click onto an individual painting and get a clearcut colour image. It is unbelievable," he said. "Now everything is clustered together on the one site."

The magazine has been instrumental over the past eight years in tracking down over 20 million pounds ($33 million) worth of stolen art works. They range from antique furniture to jewellery, paintings and sculptures.
